Thanks — this is exactly the right time to align. I put together a short
certification pathway and an initial evidence checklist (attached):

1) Acceptance matrix (what Acme Security needs vs what Redwood can produce)

Adding a few operational constraints based on the private runtime:

- Egress: TLS outbound on 443 to the HEC endpoint is standard. If Acme wants
  mutual TLS, we support client certs; you'll need to provide rotation windows
  for cert renewal.
- Ports: no additional ports required for logs/metrics. Traces use existing
  collector TLS channel.
- KV/cache: our runtime may persist short-lived KV entries for prefix caching;
  no PII is stored by default — we can produce a config flag and config diff.
- Audit trail: we emit forwarder-level delivery receipts (message id, timestamp,
  downstream ack). We'll include examples in the evidence bundle.

I'll produce the firewall rule snippets (expected ACL rules + sample iptables)
and attach as part of the Week 1 deliverables.

-karthik

Dropping the HEC onramp diagram (attached) and callouts:

- Onramp supports token-based HEC and mTLS. For air-gapped customer setups we
  recommend running an outbound-only forwarder VM inside their enclave with a
  short-lived mTLS cert.
- We will rotate HEC tokens every 7 days for audit-friendly rotation; logs showing
  rotation events will be included in the bundle.
- Payloads are gzipped JSON; Splunk HEC index mapping lives in the attached
  diagram notes.

Ben

Short operational notes for the runbook we'll hand off at the end of Week 3:

- Evidence bundle structure: 1) configs, 2) network ACL snippets, 3) rotation logs,

- Trace hook naming: use the service.namespace.operation pattern. We'll attach a

- Acceptance test: a simple smoke test that sends 10 traces and 100 log events
